introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics Paper 2 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Time allowed: three hours.**

Answer ALL 10 questions. For your guidance, the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated. Mathematical formulae and tables published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Show that the curve with polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ where,
$$r^{2} = \frac{36}{9 - 5\sin^{2}\theta},$$
represents an ellipse. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply out: $r^{2}\left(9 - 5\sin^{2}\theta\right) = 36$, i.e.
$$9r^{2} - 5\,(r\sin\theta)^{2} = 36.$$
Use $r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$ and $r\sin\theta = y$:
$$9(x^{2} + y^{2}) - 5y^{2} = 36 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 9x^{2} + 4y^{2} = 36 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{x^{2}}{4} + \frac{y^{2}}{9} = 1.$$
This is the Cartesian equation of an ellipse centred at the origin, with semi-axes $2$ (along the $x$-axis) and $3$ (along the $y$-axis). $\blacksquare$

(The denominator $9 - 5\sin^{2}\theta \geq 4 > 0$ for every $\theta$, so $r$ exists in every direction, as it should for a closed curve. Checks: $\theta = 0$ gives $r = 2$, and $\theta = \pi/2$ gives $r = 3$.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Find in polar form, the coordinates of the foci of this ellipse. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The ellipse $\dfrac{x^{2}}{4} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{9} = 1$ has its major axis along the $y$-axis because $9 > 4$. With $a^{2} = 9$ (semi-major) and $b^{2} = 4$ (semi-minor), the focal distance $c$ satisfies
$$c^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2} = 9 - 4 = 5 \quad\Rightarrow\quad c = \sqrt{5}.$$
The eccentricity is $e = \dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{\sqrt5}{3}$, and the foci are at $(0, \sqrt5)$ and $(0, -\sqrt5)$ in Cartesian form.

In polar form $(r, \theta)$, with $r > 0$:
$$\boxed{\left(\sqrt{5},\ \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \quad\text{and}\quad \left(\sqrt{5},\ \tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)}$$
(the second may also be written $\left(\sqrt5, -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, or equivalently $\left(-\sqrt5, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$).
